---
title: "Grounding AI in real sources: what a retrieval tool fixes, and what it cannot"
subtitle: "About 70 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-tip title="In short"}
- **The idea.** A tool that answers only from documents you give it rarely
  invents a reference, because every citation points at a passage it was
  handed. You can now use one to read a set of papers fast, and check any
  sentence from it in about a minute.
- **What you do.** Load four papers into Gemini Notebook (formerly
  NotebookLM), ask for a one-page journal-club brief, and check three of its
  sentences against their sources.
- **What you keep.** The checked and corrected brief, and the one-minute
  check: click the citation, read a line above and below, and ask whether the
  sentence is narrower or broader than the passage.
- **Short on time?** Read "Journal club is Thursday", "What 'grounded' means,
  step by step", and "The failure grounding does not fix". Do Steps 1 and 2.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Explain what a context window is, and why a chatbot only seems to remember
   your conversation: the whole conversation is sent again every turn.
2. State plainly that a language model does not learn from you, and say what
   does change between one turn and the next.
3. Describe the six retrieval steps in order: chunk, embed, index, retrieve,
   augment, generate.
4. Explain why a tool that answers from your sources invents citations far less
   often than a general chatbot, and why that comes from how it is built rather
   than from care.
5. Catch the error that grounding does not fix: a real, correctly linked source
   that the summary has misread or stretched too far.
6. Build a notebook from sources you chose, use it to write a brief you have
   checked, and say when that is and is not a literature search.

Course competencies: AIM-1 (foundations), AIM-2 (critical appraisal), AIM-9
(research and scholarship).
:::

**What you need.** A Google account for Gemini Notebook (a personal Gmail
account works; see "Getting in" in the Do), and your university ChatGPT Edu or
Copilot account in a second tab. Nothing to install. Made-up patients only.
The time is about 15 minutes of reading, 7 of video, 35 to 40 of doing, and
10 for the check and the closing question.

## Journal club is Thursday

You are three weeks into a sub-internship. The chief resident hands you a
paper to present at Thursday's journal club, and four more "for background."
The topic is whether AI tools that answer from a set of documents are ready
for the clinic, and she knows you have opinions. It is Monday. You have five
PDFs, two call shifts, and a personal statement to finish.

A co-intern says: put them all into Gemini Notebook and ask it your questions.
(Google renamed NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook on
[16 July 2026](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-notebook/notebooklm-gemini-notebook/).
Papers and colleagues still use the old name.) A tool like this answers only
from the documents you give it. Ask it about the guideline paper and you get
something like this.

::: {.grounded-answer}
<div class="q">Did adding retrieval improve the accuracy of the language models on the guideline questions, and did it work for all the models?</div>
<div class="a">Adding guideline retrieval improved accuracy across all models, with a pooled gain of +0.64 points (95% CI 0.47–0.80) on the automated judge.<a class="cite" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/">1</a> The benefit was largest for weaker models, with Mistral, Qwen3, and GPT-OSS showing gains of +0.72 to +0.94 points, but modest or absent for already-strong models like DeepSeek and GPT-5.<a class="cite" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/">1</a> Additionally, hallucination rates plummeted from 42% to 4% consistently across all base models when retrieval was enabled.<a class="cite" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/">1</a></div>
<div class="srcs">1 · Vollmer et al., <i>Diagnostics</i> 2026 · Results, Table 6. Illustrative: not Gemini Notebook output. A different tool that also answers only from the source it is given (Claude, reading the paper's web page) wrote this on 2026-09-07; the callout "Where the opening answer came from" below has the details.</div>
:::

Every number in that answer is real. Every little blue "1" links to a passage
that exists. The first sentence is going on your slide. But the first
sentence is broader than the paper. The paper says the gain was statistically
significant in three models and only "directional" in the two strongest: a
trend that could be chance.

This chapter is about why the numbers are real, why the sentence drifted, and
how to tell in about a minute. Two words first, because vendors use both. A
**grounded** tool is one that answers from documents it was given and points
back to them. **Retrieval** is how it finds the right passages in those
documents before it writes.

## Why this matters

In residency you will read less than you do now and rely on summaries more.
Tools like this one will write many of them: a notebook built from a
rotation's reading list, a literature tool that searches PubMed, a tool inside
the EHR that answers from your hospital's protocols. Used well, they are fast
and accurate. In one study, four orthopedic specialists rated 50 disability
cases against a written regulation. With NotebookLM they were right 91% of
the time, against 68% working by hand, and finished each case more than three
times faster
[@pmid:42534267].

These tools "cite their sources", and that is a real advance. What citing
protects you from, and what it does not, follows from how the tool works.
When a notebook misreads a paper, the result is a wrong slide. When the
grounded tool inside the EHR misreads a protocol, the result can harm a
patient. The clinician who repeated the sentence is responsible for it.

## How it works

### The model has no memory

Start with something you can see. Open a chatbot and ask it who won the 2020
World Series, the baseball championship. It answers: the Dodgers. Ask "where
was it played?" It answers correctly: Arlington, Texas, because of the
pandemic. It seems to remember the first question.

It does not. Here is what the model actually received on the second turn:

```
[user]      Who won the 2020 World Series?
[assistant] The Los Angeles Dodgers won the 2020 World Series ...
[user]      Where was it played?
```

The entire conversation is sent again, every turn. The model then writes the
next piece of text given all of it. That block of text is the **context
window**: everything the model can see at the moment it answers. It is
measured in **tokens**, which are words or pieces of words, and it has a fixed
size. When you close the tab, the context is gone. The model is exactly what
it was before you opened it.

So a language model does not learn from you. Nothing you type changes the
model's **weights**, the billions of numbers set during training that make it
what it is. What changes between turns is the context. "It got better as we
talked" means "the context got longer."

Two things can look like learning, and neither is. Some chatbots, ChatGPT
among them, have a memory setting that saves notes about you and pastes them
into later chats. And the company may *store* what you type; some consumer
accounts let it train the *next* model, months later. Both are about how your
data is handled. That is why the course rule is about what you type in.

The context window has a fixed size, and the model does not read all of a
long one equally well (Go deeper has the study). A retrieval tool's whole job
is to choose the few passages that go into it.

### What "grounded" means, step by step

A general chatbot writes a reference the way it writes everything else: as
likely-looking text. That is how it can produce a reference that looks right
and does not exist. A retrieval tool searches first and writes second. The
search-first way has six steps. Together they are the **retrieval pipeline**,
and each step is a place where something can go wrong. Google does not
publish exactly how Gemini Notebook does each step. The six steps are the
general design that tools of this kind follow.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-rag-pipeline
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart in two columns. Left column, when you add a source: your PDF is chunked into passages, each passage is embedded as a list of numbers, and the numbers are indexed. Right column, when you ask a question: the question is embedded and the nearest passages are retrieved from the index, those passages are pasted into the context window, and the model generates an answer pointing at them."
%%| fig-cap: "The retrieval pipeline. The left column happens once, when you add a source. The right column happens every time you ask a question. Nothing in either column reads the paper the way you would."
flowchart LR
  accTitle: The retrieval pipeline
  accDescr: Flowchart in two columns. Left column, when you add a source, your PDF is chunked into passages, each passage is embedded as a list of numbers, and the numbers are indexed. Right column, when you ask a question, the question is embedded and the nearest passages are retrieved from the index, those passages are pasted into the context window, and the model generates an answer pointing at them.
  subgraph I["When you add a source"]
    direction TB
    doc[Your PDF] --> chunk[1. Chunk: cut into passages of a few hundred words]
    chunk --> embed[2. Embed: turn each passage into a list of numbers]
    embed --> index[3. Index: store the numbers so similar ones are findable]
  end
  subgraph Q["When you ask a question"]
    direction TB
    q[Your question] --> retrieve[4. Retrieve: embed the question, find the nearest passages]
    retrieve --> augment[5. Augment: paste those passages into the context window]
    augment --> generate[6. Generate: write an answer, pointing at the passages]
  end
  index -.-> retrieve
```

**Chunking** cuts the document into passages of a few hundred words, because
a whole paper will not fit in the context window next to your question and
forty other papers. Chunking is simple by design. It cuts on length, not
meaning.

**Embedding** turns each passage into a list of numbers, called an
**embedding**. Passages about similar things get similar numbers. "Apixaban
reduced major bleeding" and "less hemorrhage with the factor Xa inhibitor"
get numbers that are close together. "The patient's dog is named Apixaban"
does not. You do not need to know more than "similar meaning, nearby
numbers."

**Indexing** stores those numbers so that, given a new list of numbers, the
closest matches can be found in milliseconds.

**Retrieval** turns your question into numbers the same way and returns the
nearest few passages, usually between three and twenty. **Augmentation**
pastes them into the context window, in front of your question, as plain
text. Then **generation** is the ordinary thing a language model does: write
the most likely next words. The difference is that now the most likely
continuation of "according to the passages above" is something the passages
actually say. A citation is a pointer back to a passage that is already
in the window.

That is the entire method. The model did not become honest. It was given the
answer and asked to paraphrase it.

### Why grounded tools invent less

Studies that check citations often score each one on a simple scale. **2**:
the source supports the sentence. **1**: the source is real, but the sentence
misdescribes it. **0**: the source does not exist as given. In one such study
of spine-surgery questions, a tool that searches PubMed directly scored 2 on
every citation. The general chatbots did worse, and the worst made up 26% of
its references [@pmid:42232526]. The six steps above are the reason.

The guideline study from the opening measured the same effect one model at a
time [@pmid:42587692]. Five models answered 50 questions from a German
guideline on oral cavity cancer, each with and without retrieval of that
guideline. **Hallucination**, the field's word for made-up content stated as
fact, fell from 42% to 4%. Citations that pointed at a real retrieved passage
rose from none to between 51% and 89%, depending on the model.

![What retrieval changes, and by how much. The guideline study first compared
six systems. The numbers here come from its second test: five base models,
each run with and without retrieval of the guideline, on the same 50
questions. Redrawn from the reported
figures in Vollmer et al., *Diagnostics* 2026 (open access,
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)). The bar for
citations that point at a real passage shows the range across models.](../images/retrieval-hallucination-vollmer-2026.svg){#fig-vollmer fig-alt="Bar chart with two pairs of bars. Content-level hallucination: 42 percent without retrieval, 4 percent with retrieval. Citations grounded in a retrieved passage: 0 percent without retrieval, 51 to 89 percent with retrieval."}

The drop comes from how the tool is built, not from the tool being careful.
The same paper found the *accuracy* gain from retrieval was large for the
three weaker models. For the two strongest it was small and not statistically
significant. The drop in made-up content, and the gain in checkable
citations, held across all five [@pmid:42587692]. The authors add that the
strong models may simply have been near the top of the scale already. The
safer summary is this: grounding does not reliably make a model smarter. It
makes it *checkable*.

A grounded tool can also do something a general one does not: say it does
not know. A guideline chatbot for lung cancer was asked about cancers its
guideline did not cover. It "consistently declined to answer and indicated
that the available information was insufficient" [@pmid:42611847]. A general
chatbot, asked the same question, writes a paragraph. "I cannot find that in
your sources" is the sentence that tells you the tool is doing what it
claims. You can try this yourself in Step 4 of the Do.

::: {.callout-note title="These numbers move"}
Every rate above is one tool, one field, one month. When your own run in the
Do disagrees with a number here, that is expected. The pipeline in
@fig-rag-pipeline is the part that lasts.
:::

### The failure grounding does not fix

Go back to the opening answer. Its sources are real, and its numbers are in
the paper's Table 6. Its first sentence says retrieval "improved accuracy
across all models." The paper says the gain was significant for three models
and "small and not statistically significant for the already-strong bases."
The answer's second sentence half-corrects this. But the first sentence is the
one that goes on the slide.

On the 2/1/0 scale this is a **score 1**: a real reference, described more
broadly than it supports. It is the kind of error that grounding, because of
how it is built, cannot catch. The pipeline guarantees that the text came from
the passages. It does not guarantee that the model read the passages the way
the authors meant them. A dentistry study put it this way: the retrieval
systems "avoided fabricated references but still generated incorrect
interpretations" [@pmid:41266194].

The misreading usually goes one way. When 10 widely used models were asked to
summarize scientific texts, most produced conclusions broader than the
original, even when told to be accurate. Model-written summaries were nearly
five times more likely than human-written ones to contain a broad
generalization [@pmid:40309181]. "In this subgroup" becomes "in patients."
"Was associated with" becomes "improves." "Not significant for the strong
models" becomes "across all models." The summary reads better than the paper,
and that is the problem.

::: {.callout-tip title="Where the opening answer came from, and how to catch it" collapse="true" #specimen}
**The run.** On 2026-09-07 the full text of Vollmer et al., *Diagnostics*
2026 [@pmid:42587692] was given to a tool that answers only from the page it
is given. That tool was a Claude model, the one behind the web-page reader in
Claude Code. It was not Gemini Notebook. The question was the journal-club
question from the opening: *did adding retrieval improve accuracy, and did it
work for all the models?* The three sentences at the top of this chapter are
its answer, word for word. A second run on a different paper
[@pmid:42534267] produced a score-2 answer. That one kept the authors' own
caution that the tool had not been tested at other sites. The misreading is
not inevitable. It is common.

**The check.** In a notebook, clicking the citation shows you the passage.
Here, open the paper and find Table 6. Two of the five confidence intervals
cross zero, which means the gain for those two models may be nothing. That is
the whole check. Read *one line above and one line below* the passage: the
line below is where the "however" usually is.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="If you have more time: what chunking does to a table"}
Take a results table in a paper you uploaded. To the tool it is a few lines
of text. If a chunk boundary falls inside it, the tool stores something like
the block below. It is built from Table 6 of the guideline study and the
sentence that describes it. The cut and the layout are made up; it is not a
screenshot of any tool.

::: {.chunks}
<pre class="chunk"><span class="lbl">chunk 7 of 23</span>...

Table 6. Within-model effect of guideline retrieval (automated judge).

Model             Base      +RAG    Δ accuracy (95% CI)
Mistral Small     3.40      4.34    +0.94 (0.58–1.30)
Qwen3-Next        3.52      4.38    +0.86 (0.50–1.22)</pre>
<pre class="chunk"><span class="lbl">chunk 8 of 23</span>GPT-OSS-120B      3.62      4.34    +0.72 (0.36–1.08)
DeepSeek-V3.2     4.08      4.44    +0.36 (−0.01–0.72)
GPT-5-chat        4.18      4.48    +0.30 (−0.07–0.66)

The gain was large for the weaker models and small and not statistically significant for the already-strong bases ...</pre>
:::

Chunk 8 has the rows that matter for the question in the opening scenario.
Chunk 8 has no column headings. When it is retrieved alone, the model sees
five numbers per line and has to guess what they mean. When only chunk 7 is
retrieved, the model sees the headings and the two rows where retrieval
helped most. It never sees the sentence that qualifies them. Both chunks are
real. Both citations will resolve. Neither is the table.

Nothing in the basic pipeline knows that a table is a table, or that "not
statistically significant" three lines later applies to the number above it.
Better tools try to keep tables whole, and from the outside you cannot tell
how well yours does. These are errors of *reading*, made on a source that is
real.
::::

### Three more things grounding cannot see

The pipeline answers from what you gave it. That sets three limits, and no
citation link will show you any of them.

**The source set.** A confident summary of five weak papers is a confident
summary of five weak papers, with perfect citations. To trust the notebook,
you have to trust what you put in it. Judging the papers themselves is the
subject of [Critical appraisal](core-appraisal.qmd).

**What is missing.** A notebook cannot cite a paper it does not contain. It
will not tell you that the trial that would change your mind was published
last month and is not in your five PDFs. That is the difference between a
grounded search and a systematic one, a search that tries to find every
relevant paper. The tool is very good at *reading a defined set of
documents*. It is the wrong tool for *what does the literature say*, because
there the papers you failed to include are the ones that matter.

**Disagreement.** When two sources disagree, retrieval pulls passages from
both, and generation writes one paragraph. The result can be one blended
answer that no source holds, with the disagreement smoothed away. You will
test whether your tool does this in Step 3 of the Do, with two papers chosen
because they disagree about the same tool.

::: {.callout-important title="The practical rule"}
A grounded tool fixes the reference. It helps you see where each sentence
came from. It does nothing for the claim itself. So: for any sentence you will
repeat, click its citation, read a line above and below, and ask whether the
sentence is narrower or broader than the passage. Broader is the usual
direction. The tool is a way of finding your way through sources. It is not a
source. The citation on your slide is the paper, and you have now read that
part of it.
:::

**Video.** IBM Technology, "What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?",
presented by Marina Danilevsky (23 August 2023; 6 min 36 s).
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T-D1OfcDW1M>

A whiteboard version of @fig-rag-pipeline, with nothing you need to know
first. Listen for the story about which planet has the most moons. The
speaker's confident wrong answer comes from what the model learned in
training, which was out of date. Her fix, going to look it up, is retrieval.
Then notice what the video does not say: that the model can retrieve the
right passage and misread it. That gap is what this chapter covers.

**Reading alternative.** The written article this chapter is built on,
[Grounding AI in real sources](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-10-07-rag-notebooklm-idpt-8079/),
about fifteen minutes.

## Do

Made-up patients only. [What counts as patient information](../course/patient-information.qmd).
Your sources here are published papers, so nothing about a patient goes in.

::: {.callout-tip title="Getting in"}
Gemini Notebook runs in the browser at
[notebook.google](https://notebook.google/); the old NotebookLM address
redirects there. It is free with a Google account, and a personal Gmail
account works. Making a *new*
Google account may ask for a phone number; if you will not give one, use the
no-Google path below. If you sign in with a school Google account and the
tool is missing or will not load, your school has turned it off. Do not spend
time on it; switch to a personal account
[VERIFY: nobody has yet run this Do in Gemini Notebook with a CU account; confirm it loads before students try]{.verify}.

**Limits.** Google's
[plans page](https://support.google.com/notebooklm/answer/16213268) lists
50 sources per notebook on the free plan (checked 12 October 2026). Since
2 September 2026, use on personal accounts has a limit based on how much
computing your requests take, and it
[refreshes every five hours](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-notebook/new-flexible-usage-limits/).
This chapter needs far less than that.

No Google account, and you will not make one? Attach the papers in ChatGPT
Edu or Copilot and say "answer only from the attached documents." That gives
you the same *exercise* with a weaker *guarantee*, because a general chatbot
told to stay inside its sources will still use its training at times. Say
which tool you used in question 2 of your
[journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd).
:::

### Step 1: choose your sources (10 minutes)

Pick three to five papers in your own specialty that you were already going
to read. If you do not have them, find them:

```
("large language model" OR "retrieval-augmented generation")
AND <your specialty> AND free full text[filter]
```

Filter PubMed to the last three years, read three abstracts, and take the
three to five papers that share a question. "Free full text" matters because
Gemini Notebook needs the paper, not the abstract. For each one, open the PMC
version and paste its URL as a website source. That is faster than
downloading and uploading the PDF, and it works the same way.

If you have no specialty yet, or want a set chosen for this exercise, use this
ready-made set. Every paper is open access on PMC. Every one was checked in
PubMed. And they are, on purpose, about the tool you are using; they call it
by its old name, NotebookLM.

| Paper | What it is | PMC |
|---|---|---|
| Vollmer et al., *Diagnostics* 2026 [@pmid:42587692] | 50 guideline questions; five models, each with and without retrieval | [PMC13465324](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/) |
| Duran et al., *Digital Health* 2026 [@pmid:42534267] | NotebookLM for orthopedic disability rating: 91% vs 68% accuracy | [PMC13420063](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13420063/) |
| Seki et al., *Clinics and Practice* 2026 [@pmid:42645138] | NotebookLM classifying radiographs: agreement with dentists near zero | [PMC13511330](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13511330/) |
| Basu and Huynh, *BMC Health Serv Res* 2026 [@pmid:42251377] | Systematic review of 44 hallucination-mitigation studies | [PMC13470931](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13470931/) |

: A ready-made source set, already checked. Two of these papers disagree about whether NotebookLM is accurate, and they are both right. {#tbl-sources}

Make a new notebook, add the sources, and wait for each to finish processing.
That wait is steps 1 to 3 of @fig-rag-pipeline happening.

### Step 2: make a brief, then check three sentences (15 minutes)

Ask the notebook for something you would really use:

```
Make me a one-page journal-club brief from these four papers. For each
paper: the question, the design, the main result with its numbers, and
one limitation. End with where the papers agree and where they disagree.
```

If you used your own sources, change "four" to the number you added.

Read the brief. It took seconds, and most of it will be right. Your job is to
find out which parts.

Pick three sentences you would say out loud at journal club: one with a
number, one that compares papers, and one whose answer you already know. For
the ready-made set, make that last one the sentence about the guideline
study's main result; you know from the opening what the paper says. For each
sentence, click its citation. Read the highlighted passage plus one line above
and one line below. Then score it on the 2/1/0 scale from "Why grounded tools
invent less". **2** if the passage supports the sentence as written. **1** if
the passage is real but the sentence is broader, narrower, or different.
**0** if the cited passage does not exist, or is about something other than
what the sentence says.

Then correct a sentence that scored 1 or 0, so that it says what its passage
says. If all three scored 2, that is a real result too: you have checked the
sentences you will repeat, so note what made you trust them. Copy the
corrected brief into a document you keep. That page is what you take to
journal club.

### Step 3: ask what the sources disagree about (5 minutes)

Ask a question your sources answer differently. For the ready-made set, ask:
*Is NotebookLM accurate?* One paper found it raised accuracy from 68% to 91%
on a rating task done from a single written regulation. Another found its
agreement with dentists on radiographs was slight or worse. Watch what the
tool does with that. Does it present both, with the task each one measured?
Or does it produce a sentence like "NotebookLM shows promise but has
limitations," which is true of everything and cites both?

### Step 4: ask what the sources cannot answer, then ask the chatbot (5 minutes)

Ask the notebook something its sources cannot support: a statistic that is
not in them, a named trial that is not there, a population none of the papers
studied. For the ready-made set: *What is the fabrication rate of NotebookLM
on citations in cardiology?* No source contains that. A grounded tool should
say so, or give a short answer that says what its sources do and do not
cover.

Now ask the identical question in ChatGPT Edu. Ask it the way you asked the
notebook. Compare on one thing only: **can you check where each sentence came
from?** The chatbot's answer may be better written and more useful. That is
not the thing you are comparing.

ChatGPT Edu searches the web, so it may answer with links. That is a
different question about where the answer came from. The page is real.
Whether it is evidence is the subject of
[Critical appraisal](core-appraisal.qmd).

### Record it

```
Tool: Gemini Notebook / other: ____________     Date: __________
Sources (with PMC IDs or titles): ______________________________________

Three sentences I checked, with scores (2, 1, or 0):
  1 ______________________________________________________  score __
  2 ______________________________________________________  score __
  3 ______________________________________________________  score __

The sentence I corrected (or "all three matched", and why I trust them):
  Before: ______________________________________________________________
  After:  ______________________________________________________________

Disagreement question: did the tool present both positions, or smooth them?
________________________________________________________________________

Question the sources cannot answer. What I asked: _____________________
  Notebook said: ________________________________________________________
  Chatbot said:  ________________________________________________________
  Which one could I trace, sentence by sentence? _______________________
```

Keep the corrected brief. You know which of its sentences you have read
against the paper, and you can say *how* any wrong one was stretched. That is
the skill; a count like "three of twelve citations were stretched" will
change next month. What you checked, how, and what you found is question 2
of your [learning journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd).

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| The no-memory explanation | You can say what is re-sent each turn and why a new chat starts from zero, without the word "memory" | "It remembers the conversation" |
| The no-learning statement | You can say what changes between turns (the context) and what does not (the model), and separate that from where your text is stored | "It learns from what you type" |
| The pipeline | Six steps in order, and what each one does in a sentence | Fewer than six, or "it searches the documents" |
| Why the citations are real | You can say why a citation from a grounded tool points at a passage, and why that is not the same as the model being careful | "It's more accurate" |
| Your brief | Three sentences clicked and scored, each beside its passage; one corrected, or a reason all three stand | Scores given by reading the brief alone |
| The disagreement result | You can say whether the tool presented both sources or smoothed them, and quote the smoothing sentence if it did | "It handled it fine" |
| The contrast with the chatbot | Both answers recorded; you can say which one you could trace and why the other reads better anyway | Only the notebook's answer |
| The search limit | You can say in one sentence when a grounded notebook is not a literature search | "It's good for research" |

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Answer in writing before
you close this chapter. Two specifics. First: the next time a summary with
citations is put in front of you, from a notebook, an EHR tool, or a
co-intern, what is the one-minute check you will do before repeating a
sentence from it? Which of the failures in this chapter does that check
catch? Second: go back to Monday. The five PDFs are in the notebook, the first
sentence of its answer is on your draft slide, and journal club is Thursday.
What do you change on the slide? What do you say when the chief asks how you
prepared? What do you do with the two papers that disagree? One word is not
an answer to any of these.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The overgeneralization study, 10 models and 4,900 summaries
  [@pmid:40309181]. It found newer models did worse than older ones.
- The guideline-retrieval study behind @fig-vollmer, whose pipeline was
  released openly [@pmid:42587692], and a systematic review that compares
  retrieval with other ways to reduce made-up content [@pmid:42251377].
- Two studies of NotebookLM itself: one where it helped [@pmid:42534267] and
  one where it was the wrong tool for an image task [@pmid:42645138]. Read
  them as a pair.
- The dentistry comparison: retrieval systems "avoided fabricated references
  but still generated incorrect interpretations" [@pmid:41266194].
- "Lost in the middle" [@doi:10.1162/tacl_a_00638]. Researchers moved the one
  relevant document among many others. Models answered best when it sat at
  the start or the end of the context, and worse when it was in the middle.
  A long context window does not mean the model reads all of it well.
- A two-day workshop for clinicians that limits citation generation to
  NotebookLM and then makes participants check every one. It says plainly
  that whether this reduces fabrication was not tested [@pmid:42684317].

**Talks**

- [Grounding AI in real sources](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-10-07-rag-notebooklm-idpt-8079/):
  the written article this chapter is built on, with the conversation shown
  as raw text.
- [Word embeddings as the basis for LLMs](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-12-word-embeddings-basis-for-llms/):
  what "similar meaning, nearby numbers" means, with an interactive embedding
  projector.
- [Prompt engineering](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-17-prompt-engineering/):
  ten rules with clinical examples, if your brief came back vague. The
  [prompting lab](enrichment-prompting-lab.qmd) is built on it.
